Expand “Question, prerequisites and sources” to see what it covers, which tools it uses, and its references in the same place. 01Understand the phenomenon Use diagrams, conservation, and dimensions. 02Formulate the equations Track assumptions, scaling, and boundaries. 03Solve and check Explore solutions and their limits. Mathematical preparation Calculus, introductory ordinary differential equations, vectors, and matrices. The treatment introduces partial differential equations through conservation laws, followed by linearization, nondimensionalization, and similarity transformations. The foundational chapters on the virial theorem, stellar structure, and cosmic expansion provide useful physical context. AREA 01 Equilibrium and limits of stars and clouds From the foundational virial theorem and white dwarfs to the internal structure of spheres and filaments. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ 01 Lane–Emden equation and polytropes Solve a stellar interior and recover the coefficient of the Chandrasekhar mass. 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Lane–Emden equation and polytropes TOOLS Calculus, the chain rule, and introductory ordinary differential equations READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How does a pressure–density relation determine stellar mass and radius? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Reduce hydrostatic balance and mass conservation to a dimensionless equation. Connect central regularity, the surface zero, and the n = 3 model to the Chandrasekhar mass. Read the chapter → Reference: Princeton · Polytropes ↗ 02 Bonnor–Ebert spheres and a cloud’s limiting mass How much self-gravity can a pressure-confined isothermal cloud support? 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Bonnor–Ebert spheres and external pressure TOOLS The Lane–Emden chapter, ODEs, exponentials, and nondimensionalization READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION When does an externally compressed isothermal gas cloud become unstable? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Truncate an isothermal sphere at a specified external pressure and follow equilibrium sequences. State the quantities held fixed when assessing stability. Read the chapter → Reference: Bonnor (1956) ↗ 03 Ostriker’s isothermal cylinder and critical line mass Remembering J. P. Ostriker through an analytic model of filament gravity and its limiting mass per length. 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Ostriker’s isothermal cylinder and critical line mass TOOLS Hydrostatic balance, Gauss’s law, differentiation and integration READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How much mass per unit length can a long gaseous filament support? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive an analytic equilibrium from cylindrical Gauss’s law and hydrostatic balance. Connect the flat centre, r⁻⁴ envelope and line mass 2cₛ²/G, distinguishing pressure truncation and projected column density. A chapter remembering J. P. Ostriker. Read the chapter → Reference: Ostriker (1964), §III, equations (56)–(61) ↗ 04 Hayashi limit and Hayashi tracks Why can a contracting pre-main-sequence star fade at nearly constant effective temperature? 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Hayashi limit and Hayashi tracks TOOLS Lane–Emden, ideal gas, calculus and powers READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why can a contracting pre-main-sequence star fade at nearly constant effective temperature? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Connect an n = 3/2 polytrope to approximate full convection, photospheric boundary conditions, and H⁻ opacity. Use L = 4πR²σT_eff⁴ to read the contracting track, separating the atmospheric physics setting the Hayashi limit from the energy budget setting its timescale. Distinguish Henyey tracks when a radiative core develops. Read the chapter → Reference: Princeton · Hayashi limit ↗ AREA 02 Rotation and nonspherical gravitational equilibrium Move beyond spheres and connect shape to motion along different axes. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ 05 Gravitational potentials of ellipsoids At fixed mass, how does flattening or elongation change the internal gravity? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Gravitational potentials of ellipsoids TOOLS Newtonian gravity, integration and Poisson’s equation READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION At fixed mass, how does flattening or elongation change the internal gravity? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Begin with homogeneous ellipsoids, relating their potentials to axis ratios and comparing axisymmetric and triaxial shapes. Read the chapter → Reference: Binney · Dynamics of elliptical galaxies ↗ 06 Tensor virial theorem and Maclaurin/Jacobi sequences Which rotating fluid shapes can be in equilibrium, and are they stable? 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Tensor virial theorem and Maclaurin/Jacobi sequences TOOLS The ellipsoid chapter, matrices and equations of motion READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Which rotating fluid shapes can be in equilibrium, and are they stable? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use directional balances to study spheroidal and triaxial fluid figures. Separate equilibrium, bifurcation, and stability, and distinguish fluid figures from stellar systems. Read the chapter → Reference: Lebovitz (1961) ↗ AREA 03 Gravitational instability and cosmic structure Separate background from perturbations and ask which disturbances grow. Connect to foundations: Cosmic expansion and the Hubble–Lemaître law ↗ 07 Jeans instability and the Jeans swindle Derive the wavelengths dominated by gravity and inspect the treatment of the uniform background. 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Jeans instability and the Jeans swindle TOOLS Fluid conservation, partial derivatives, linearization, and plane waves READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Which wavelengths can pressure stabilize, and how should the gravity of a uniform background be treated? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Linearize continuity, momentum, and Poisson equations to obtain a dispersion relation. Compare a static background assumption with an expanding cosmological background. Read the chapter → Reference: Falco et al. · Why does the Jeans swindle work? ↗ 08 Zel’dovich approximation and pancakes Why does gravitational clustering not necessarily begin by forming spheres? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Zel’dovich approximation and pancakes TOOLS Cosmic expansion, mass conservation, derivatives and determinants READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why does gravitational clustering not necessarily begin by forming spheres? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use a Lagrangian map and mass conservation to obtain density and study one-axis compression. Explain the breakdown at shell crossing. Read the chapter → Reference: Zel’dovich (1970) ↗ 09 Press–Schechter theory and the halo mass function Count cosmic density fluctuations to predict the abundance of dark-matter halos by mass. 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Press–Schechter theory and the halo mass function TOOLS Cosmic expansion and Jeans chapters, calculus, normal distributions, and logarithms READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How can initial density fluctuations predict halo abundances by mass? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive the linear spherical-collapse threshold, relate Gaussian tails to mass fractions, and explain cloud-in-cloud accounting and the factor of two. Obtain the mass function and power-law self-similarity, with limits for galaxy formation. Read the chapter → Reference: Press & Schechter (1974) ↗ 35 Lin–Mestel–Shu: collapse of a uniform spheroid How does a small departure from spherical shape grow during pressure-free collapse? 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Lin–Mestel–Shu: collapse of a uniform spheroid TOOLS Ellipsoidal gravity, ordinary differential equations, and mass conservation READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How does a small departure from spherical shape grow during pressure-free collapse? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use the interior field of a homogeneous ellipsoid and mass conservation to derive and integrate the two axis equations. Read the chapter → Reference: Lin, Mestel & Shu (1965) ↗ AREA 04 Instabilities of fluid interfaces Use small interface disturbances to study buoyancy, shear-driven growth, and the onset of mixing. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ 10 Rayleigh–Taylor instability How does a small interface disturbance grow when denser fluid is above lighter fluid? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Rayleigh–Taylor instability TOOLS Partial derivatives, complex exponentials, linearization, and fluid momentum READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How quickly does an interface deform when denser fluid is above lighter fluid? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive ω² = −Agk from potential flow and kinematic/pressure conditions. Examine Atwood number, growth time, short wavelengths, and the distinction from nonlinear mixing. Read the chapter → Reference: Maryland · Hydrodynamics ↗ 11 Kelvin–Helmholtz instability Velocity shear feeds interface waves and, later, vortices. 25 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Kelvin–Helmholtz instability TOOLS Interface conditions from the RT chapter, complex numbers, dispersion relations READING TIME 25 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why does a velocity difference along an interface amplify waves? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Include advection in interface conditions, derive the dispersion relation, and separate wave drift from growth. Compare density contrast, gravity, and finite shear thickness. Read the chapter → Reference: MIT · Interfacial phenomena ↗ AREA 05 Fluids, similarity solutions, and high-energy radiation Study blast waves and collapse with similarity solutions, then connect shocks to particle acceleration and radiation. Connect to foundations: Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation ↗ 12 Bondi accretion and the sonic point Use mass conservation and a pressure gradient to select a critical inflow. 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Bondi accretion and the sonic point TOOLS ODEs, logarithms, and steady-flow conservation READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How does gas from a quiet surrounding medium flow toward a central object? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use steady spherical mass and momentum conservation to derive r_B = GM/c_s,∞² and the sonic point. Pair the isothermal model with Parker wind, then examine how outer density, sound speed, and heat-capacity ratio select adiabatic accretion. Distinguish free-fall estimates from a transonic critical solution. Read the chapter → Reference: Bondi (1952) ↗ 13 Parker wind and transonic outflow How can a hot atmosphere accelerate outward against gravity? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Parker wind and transonic outflow TOOLS The Bondi chapter, derivatives, logarithms, and boundary conditions READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How does a hot stellar atmosphere escape gravity and become a supersonic wind? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive the steady spherical isothermal wind equation (u−c_s²/u)du/dr = 2c_s²/r−GM/r² and select a regular transonic branch at r_s = GM/(2c_s²). Connect to Bondi accretion, boundary conditions, the heating needed to maintain isothermality, and magnetic effects in the real solar wind. Read the chapter → Reference: Parker (1958) ↗ 14 Sedov–Taylor blast waves From the two-fifths scaling to internal profiles and the energy integral. 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Sedov–Taylor and Rankine–Hugoniot conditions TOOLS Calculus, partial derivatives and the chain rule, ideal gases READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How does a blast radius grow given an explosion energy and ambient density? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive shock jump conditions from conservation, then use dimensional analysis and similarity variables to solve the internal profiles. State strong-shock and energy-conservation assumptions. Read the chapter → Reference: Taylor (1950) ↗ 15 Larson–Penston and Shu isothermal collapse Why do the same isothermal gas equations admit different collapse solutions? 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Larson–Penston and Shu isothermal collapse TOOLS Bondi and Lane–Emden, partial derivatives and similarity scaling READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why do the same isothermal gas equations admit different collapse solutions? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Apply similarity transformations to spherical gas dynamics and examine sonic points and initial/boundary conditions. Do not identify the two solutions as automatically successive stages. Read the chapter → Reference: Shu (1977) ↗ 16 Shocks and particle acceleration Derive a nonthermal power law from repeated gains and escape. 25 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Shocks and particle acceleration TOOLS Logarithms, geometric sequences, probability, and shock jump conditions READING TIME 25 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why do particles cycling across a shock acquire a power-law energy distribution? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Connect shock compression to first-order Fermi gains and escape probability. Distinguish acceleration time, confinement, and cooling limits. Read the chapter → Reference: Maryland · Particle acceleration ↗ 17 Synchrotron radiation and electron cooling Translate accelerated electron energies into radio and X-ray spectra. 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Synchrotron radiation and electron cooling TOOLS Lorentz factor, scaling, calculus, and the Thomson cross section READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How do accelerated electrons and magnetic fields shape radio and X-ray spectra? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Compute characteristic frequency, power, and cooling time, translate electron power laws into light spectra, and derive a continuous-injection cooling break. Read the chapter → Reference: NRAO · Synchrotron radiation ↗ AREA 06 Statistical mechanics and relaxation of star clusters From individual orbits to evolving distributions and energy transport. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ 18 Two-body relaxation and gravitational encounters When do accumulated weak gravitational encounters significantly change an orbit? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Two-body relaxation and gravitational encounters TOOLS Virial theorem, gravitational scattering and random walks READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION When do accumulated weak gravitational encounters significantly change an orbit? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Connect encounter estimates and a random walk to relaxation time. Distinguish this process from direct stellar collisions and isolated two-body orbits. Read the chapter → Reference: Yale · Astrophysical flows ↗ 19 Fokker–Planck equation How do drift and diffusion from encounters describe changes in a distribution? 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Fokker–Planck equation TOOLS Two-body relaxation, probability density and partial derivatives READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How do drift and diffusion from encounters describe changes in a distribution? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Start with drift and diffusion in a one-variable model, then introduce orbit averaging and self-consistent gravity for clusters. Specify the distribution and conservation laws. Read the chapter → Reference: Cohn (1979) ↗ 20 Gravothermal catastrophe Why can a core heat up and contract as it transfers energy outward? 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Gravothermal catastrophe TOOLS Virial, Bonnor–Ebert and two-body relaxation chapters READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why can a core heat up and contract as it transfers energy outward? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Connect negative heat capacity with relaxation-driven transport. Examine thermodynamic constraints, binary heating, and post-collapse oscillations. Read the chapter → Reference: Lynden-Bell & Wood (1968) ↗ AREA 07 Disk transport and gravitational instability Start with angular-momentum transport, then connect accretion, winds, alpha, MRI, and self-gravity. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ 21 Angular-momentum transport and accretion What must orbiting gas transfer, and where, in order to accrete? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Angular-momentum transport and accretion TOOLS Circular motion, energy and angular-momentum conservation, basic derivatives READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Where must gas transfer angular momentum in order to accrete? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use circular-orbit j = √(GMr) to establish the requirement for accretion. Check total angular momentum and orbital energy with two rings, distinguish radial stress transport from wind removal, and build the steady torque budget leading to alpha and MRI. Read the chapter → Reference: Princeton · Accretion disks ↗ 22 Alpha disks and viscous-type accretion Parametrize transport and connect disk thickness, accretion rate, and luminosity. 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Thin disks and the Shakura–Sunyaev alpha model TOOLS Angular-momentum transport, calculus, and Keplerian rotation READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How must a rotating gas redistribute angular momentum to accrete? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Estimate the scale height from vertical balance and introduce effective viscosity ν = αc_sH. Explain that alpha parametrizes transport efficiency rather than determining its physical cause. Read the chapter → Reference: Chambers (2009) · Viscous disk model ↗ 23 MRI: magnetic fields and differential rotation Weak magnetic tension can destabilize a disk that is hydrodynamically stable. 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Balbus–Hawley instability: MRI TOOLS Angular-momentum transport, linearization, determinants, and quadratic equations READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why can a weak magnetic field destabilize a differentially rotating disk that is hydrodynamically stable? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use magnetic tension and angular-momentum exchange to introduce magnetorotational instability. In local axisymmetric ideal MHD with vertical field, derive the dispersion relation and growth when Ω decreases outward. Examine the Keplerian maximum growth rate 3Ω/4, the link to alpha transport, and nonideal effects in poorly ionized protoplanetary disks. Read the chapter → Reference: Balbus & Hawley (1991) ↗ 24 Lynden–Bell–Pringle viscous-disk similarity solutions Why can a disk spread outward while mass accretes toward the centre? 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Lynden–Bell–Pringle viscous-disk similarity solutions TOOLS Transport and alpha-disk chapters, partial derivatives and integration READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why can a disk spread outward while mass accretes toward the centre? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive surface-density evolution from mass and angular-momentum conservation. Prescribe radial viscosity to obtain similarity solutions and track accretion and outward angular-momentum transport. Read the chapter → Reference: Lynden-Bell & Pringle (1974) ↗ 25 Toomre Q and disk self-gravity Read the competition between pressure, rotation, and gravity at each wavelength. 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Toomre Q, cooling, and disk fragmentation TOOLS The Jeans chapter, linearization, rotating frames, and completing the square READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Can pressure and rotation resist self-gravity, and must an unstable disk fragment? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive Q from a local dispersion relation for a thin gas disk. Distinguish axisymmetric linear stability from nonlinear fragmentation with cooling. Read the chapter → Reference: Gammie (2001) ↗ AREA 08 Ionization, scattering, and observing cosmic gas Use light–gas interactions to measure ionized regions and galaxy-cluster pressure. Connect to foundations: Atomic light and starlight: why 10.2 eV? ↗ 26 Strömgren spheres and ionization fronts Count photons to find the size and early growth of an ionized region around a star. 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Strömgren spheres, ionization, and recombination TOOLS Volumes, exponentials, and a first-order ODE READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How large an ionized hydrogen region can a star maintain? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH For uniform, pure-hydrogen, ionization-bounded gas, derive the equilibrium radius from Q_H = (4π/3)R_S³α_B n_e n_p. Examine recombination time, case B and local reabsorption, photon escape, and dust absorption. Distinguish static balance from the initial ionization front and later pressure-driven expansion. Read the chapter → Reference: Strömgren (1939) ↗ 27 Inverse Compton scattering and the SZ effect The pressure imprint of hot galaxy-cluster electrons on the cosmic microwave background. 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Inverse Compton scattering and the Sunyaev–Zel’dovich effect TOOLS Thomson scattering, the Planck spectrum, exponential derivatives, and line-of-sight integrals READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How does hot cluster gas change the CMB, and what can that tell us? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Build y from scattering optical depth and electron temperature, then connect it to integrated electron pressure. Derive the thermal spectrum, low-frequency deficit, and approximately 217 GHz null from the Kompaneets limit. Distinguish kinetic SZ and limitations from relativistic corrections. Read the chapter → Reference: Carlstrom, Holder & Reese (2002) ↗ AREA 09 Neutron stars and pulsar magnetospheres Count the charge required by rotation and magnetic fields, then connect to acceleration and radiation. Connect to foundations: The classical electron radius and Thomson scattering ↗ 28 Goldreich–Julian density and corotation What charge density is needed in the magnetosphere of a rotating neutron star? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Goldreich–Julian density and corotation TOOLS Electromagnetism, Gauss’s law and vector products READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION What charge density is needed in the magnetosphere of a rotating neutron star? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use corotation E = −(Ω×r)×B and Gauss’s law to derive ρ_GJ ≈ −2ε₀Ω·B in SI, in a flat-spacetime quasistatic approximation neglecting the current term. Distinguish n_GJ = |ρ_GJ|/e from the total electron–positron density. Connect to the light cylinder and charge-starved acceleration gaps without extending the approximation throughout the magnetosphere. Read the chapter → Reference: Goldreich & Julian (1969) ↗ AREA 10 Nonequilibrium and multicomponent astrophysics Temperatures, magnetic fields, neutrals, and chemical composition need not adjust together. Compare relaxation, diffusion, and reaction clocks with dynamics. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ 29 Two-temperature plasmas and electron–ion relaxation How can electrons and ions in the same gas have different temperatures? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Two-temperature plasmas and electron–ion relaxation TOOLS Ideal gases, heat capacities, exponentials, and first-order ODEs READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How can electrons and ions in the same gas have different temperatures? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive temperature exchange from heat capacities and energy conservation. Supply a Coulomb exchange time, follow relaxation, and compare with a flow clock. Read the chapter → Reference: Vink et al. (2015) ↗ 30 Ambipolar diffusion: magnetic fields and neutral gas When can a magnetic field slip relative to weakly ionized gas? 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Ambipolar diffusion: magnetic fields and neutral gas TOOLS Lorentz force, pressure, diffusion, and free-fall time READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION When can a magnetic field slip relative to weakly ionized gas? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Balance Lorentz force and ion–neutral drag to derive a diffusivity and timescale. Smooth a linear magnetic perturbation and compare with a gravitational clock. Read the chapter → Reference: Hillier (2024) ↗ 31 Three-body chemistry and molecular hydrogen formation Why does high density accelerate three-body formation of molecular hydrogen? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Three-body chemistry and molecular hydrogen formation TOOLS Reaction equations, number density, separation of variables, and free-fall time READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why does high density accelerate three-body formation of molecular hydrogen? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Count H + H + H → H₂ + H, conserve nuclei, and solve for the molecular fraction. Supply the quantum-chemical rate and compare reaction and gravitational times. Read the chapter → Reference: Forrey (2013), equation (6) ↗ AREA 11 Relativistic spacetimes and orbits Start from a metric and follow the clocks, light, and particle motion it predicts. Connect to foundations: An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity ↗ 32 Schwarzschild: clocks, the photon sphere, and the ISCO How do the horizon, photon sphere, and innermost stable circular orbit differ within one spacetime? 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Schwarzschild: clocks, the photon sphere, and the ISCO TOOLS Foundational relativity, derivatives, conservation laws, and circular motion READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How do the horizon, photon sphere, and innermost stable circular orbit differ within one spacetime? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Read static proper time from the metric, then combine conserved quantities and normalization into an effective potential. Use derivatives and algebra to distinguish the photon sphere at 3GM/c² from the ISCO at 6GM/c². Read the chapter → Reference: Carroll · General Relativity, §7 ↗ 33 Kerr: rotation, the ergoregion, and the ISCO How does rotation change the region forbidding static observers and the stable circular orbits? 45 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Kerr: rotation, the ergoregion, and the ISCO TOOLS Schwarzschild geometry, derivatives, and conserved quantities READING TIME 45 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How does rotation change the region forbidding static observers and the stable circular orbits? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive allowed angular velocities from the metric, then use the equatorial radial potential to compare prograde and retrograde ISCOs. Read the chapter → Reference: Bardeen, Press & Teukolsky (1972) ↗ 34 Tomimatsu–Sato: Ernst potentials and the quadrupole Can vacuum spacetimes with the same mass and angular momentum differ from Kerr? 45 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Tomimatsu–Sato: Ernst potentials and the quadrupole TOOLS Kerr geometry, complex numbers, and series expansions READING TIME 45 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Can vacuum spacetimes with the same mass and angular momentum differ from Kerr? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Start from the δ = 2 Ernst potential, extract the first multipoles from axis data, and examine the ring-singularity condition.
